parts.label: (a)
parts.text: With reference to velocity and acceleration, describe uniform circular motion.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the word uniform tells you about the size of the velocity, and what moving in a circle tells you about its direction moment by moment.
Hint 2: If velocity is changing, there must be acceleration. Think about which way that acceleration must point to keep the object on a circle without speeding it up or slowing it down.
parts.proper_answer: Speed (magnitude of velocity) is constant. Velocity direction changes continuously, always tangential to the circle. Acceleration is towards the centre, perpendicular to the velocity at all times.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out speed versus velocity**
You are sitting beside me, so let us be very clear. Speed is just how fast, a scalar. Velocity is how fast plus which way, a vector. In uniform circular motion the how fast part stays the same, so $v$ is constant in magnitude. But the which way part is always changing as the object goes round.

Step 2: **See why acceleration must be sideways**
A change in velocity means acceleration, even if speed does not change. Here the change is purely in direction. To change direction without changing speed, the push must be sideways to the motion. So the acceleration is always at $90^{\circ}$ to the velocity, pointing towards the centre of the circle. This is centripetal acceleration.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Two cars are moving around a horizontal circular track. One car follows path $X$ and the other follows path $Y$, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1 (not to scale)

The radius of path $X$ is $318\text{ m}$. Path $Y$ is parallel to, and $27\text{ m}$ outside, path $X$. Both cars have mass $790\text{ kg}$. The maximum lateral (sideways) friction force $F$ that the cars can experience without sliding is the same for both cars.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
The maximum speed at which the car on path $X$ can move around the track without sliding is $94\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate $F$.

markscheme_points.text: F = mv^2 / r or v = r omega and F = mr omega^2

hints: Hint 1: Identify what provides the sideways force to keep the car on the circle, and list the values you know for mass, speed and radius for path X.
Hint 2: Recall how centripetal force links $F$, $m$, $v$ and $r$, then substitute $m = 790\text{ kg}$, $v = 94\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $r = 318\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the physics that keeps the car turning**
To stay on the circular path the car needs a resultant force towards the centre. On a flat track this is provided by lateral friction. At maximum speed without sliding, friction is at its limiting value $F$. So $F$ equals the required centripetal force.

Step 2: **Calculate with $F = mv^2/r$**
The centripetal force is: $$F = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$ Put in the numbers for path X: $$F = \frac{790 \times (94)^2}{318}$$ $$F = \frac{790 \times 8836}{318} \approx 2.20 \times 10^4\text{ N}$$ So $F \approx 2.2 \times 10^4\text{ N}$ to 2 significant figures.

hints: Hint 1: Identify what provides the sideways force to keep the car on the circle, and list the values you know for mass, speed and radius for path X.
Hint 2: Recall how centripetal force links $F$, $m$, $v$ and $r$, then substitute $m = 790\text{ kg}$, $v = 94\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $r = 318\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Both cars move around the track. Each car has the maximum speed at which it can move without sliding.

Complete Table 1.1, by placing one tick in each row, to indicate how the quantities indicated for the car on path $Y$ compare with the car on path $X$.

Table 1.1

|  | Y less than X | Y same as X | Y greater than X |
| centripetal acceleration |  |  |  |
| maximum speed |  |  |  |
| time taken for one lap of the track |  |  |  |

markscheme_points.text: time taken for one lap of the track: greater

hints: Hint 1: Start with centripetal acceleration. Both cars have the same mass and the same limiting friction force, so compare $a = F/m$ for X and Y.
Hint 2: For maximum speed, rearrange $F = mv^2/r$ to make $v$ the subject and think about what happens when $r$ gets larger from X to Y while $F$ and $m$ stay fixed.
Hint 3: For lap time, think of distance divided by speed, $T = 2\pi r / v$. Both $r$ and $v$ increase for Y, so decide which effect wins by substituting $v$ proportional to $\sqrt{r}$.
parts.proper_answer: centripetal acceleration: Y same as X. maximum speed: Y greater than X. time taken for one lap: Y greater than X.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Centripetal acceleration stays the same**
Acceleration follows Newton's second law: $$a = \frac{F}{m}$$ Both cars have $m = 790\text{ kg}$ and the same maximum $F$. So $a$ at the limit is identical. Y same as X.

Step 2: **Maximum speed is greater on the larger radius**
Rearrange $F = mv^2/r$ for $v$: $$v = \sqrt{\frac{Fr}{m}}$$ With $F$ and $m$ fixed, $v$ is proportional to $\sqrt{r}$. Path Y has radius $318 + 27 = 345\text{ m}$, larger than X. So to need the same $F$, Y can go faster. Y greater than X.

Step 3: **Lap time is greater on the larger radius**
Time for one lap is circumference over speed: $$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$$ Substitute $v$ from Step 2: $$T = \frac{2\pi r}{\sqrt{Fr/m}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{mr}{F}}$$ So $T$ is proportional to $\sqrt{r}$. Larger $r$ means larger $T$, because the extra distance wins over the extra speed. Y greater than X.
